title: Tier I Checkpoint — A Model Lesson

pts: The lesson's level, pace and cultural framing come directly from the learner profile built in Unit 2 — not from a generic coursebook default.
A recorded motivation type (instrumental or integrative) shapes how the lesson's purpose is framed to the class.
Needs analysis isn't a step you finish before planning — it's the first input into the plan itself.

v: Learner profile passports (Unit 2); class diagnostic grid

items: Look at the class diagnostic grid. Most learners are around A2 for listening and speaking; a small group is still A1 in writing.
Check the language portraits: the class shares Kannada; several learners also speak Urdu and Telugu.
Note from the ‘stop, start, continue’ slips that learners asked for more pair work and less reading aloud.
Decide: the lesson will use a local neighbourhood familiar to everyone; Kannada may be used for brief checks; pairs will mix confident and less confident speakers.
Write the can-do aim and prepare an A1-friendly writing frame for the exit ticket.
For adults, change the topic to ‘directions to my workplace’.
For a higher level, the aim becomes ‘recommend places in my neighbourhood and give reasons’.
Support: plan a map with pictures and labels for learners at A1.
Stretch: plan an extension question for fast finishers (What would you change about your neighbourhood?).

blocks.x: Profile notes turned into planning decisions:

lines: Profile: ‘Speaking in front of the class is hard’ (many learners). → Decision: pairs first, volunteers only for whole-class sharing.
Profile: strong listening, weaker writing. → Decision: listening input first; short, framed writing at the end.
Profile: shared home language. → Decision: permit a short Kannada check of instructions.

body: Purpose: to show profile information feeding planning decisions. Content: on the left, a small stack of learner passports. Three arrows lead right to three decision cards: ‘Topic: our neighbourhood’, ‘Grouping: mixed pairs’, ‘Support: writing frame for A1’. Style: clean, friendly. Board version: not applicable.

items: Google Sheets (free). If profiles and diagnostic scores are kept in a spreadsheet, sort by skill score to plan pairings quickly.

blocks.x: The paper diagnostic grid and passports, spread out on the desk while planning.

pts: Open with a short, graded listening extract to activate schema and introduce the target language in natural context.
Set a gist-level task on the first listen, then a detail-level task on the second — never both at once.
This single stage does the work of Unit 3's pre- and while-listening design in miniature.

v: The teacher’s description below; a simple map drawn on the board with empty boxes

items: Write the aim on the board. Draw a simple street map with six empty boxes.
Gist (first hearing). ‘Do I like my neighbourhood?’ Tell the description naturally.
Detail (second hearing). Learners copy the map and write the names of places in the boxes as they hear them.
Pairs compare maps. Check together by eliciting (Unit 7).
Ask one personal question: ‘Is your neighbourhood like mine?’ Learners answer in a word or two.
Use a recorded description by a colleague for a different voice.
Use a real local map, simplified.
Support: provide the six place names as a list to choose from.
Stretch: learners also note one adjective for each place.

lines: I live in a busy neighbourhood near the old market. There’s a bus stop at the end of my road, next to a small temple. Opposite the bus stop, there’s a pharmacy. I go there a lot! Between the pharmacy and the post office, there’s a tea stall. The tea is very good. There’s a park behind the post office, where children play cricket in the evening. And there’s a school on the corner, next to the park. It’s noisy in the morning, but I like it. Everything I need is close.

body: Purpose: the listening worksheet and board map. Content: a simple street plan: one main road running left to right, a side road going up. Six empty rectangles in positions matching the description (bus stop, temple, pharmacy, tea stall, post office, park, school). A small compass rose. Style: bird’s-eye line drawing, uncluttered. Board version: rectangles and roads in chalk.

items: Vocaroo (free). Record the description once so the second hearing is identical.

blocks.x: Read the description aloud at the same pace each time.

pts: Pull one or two pronunciation features directly from the listening extract — a stress pattern, a linked phrase.
Use the phonemic chart briefly rather than a full pronunciation lesson; this is noticing, not a unit of its own.
The goal is intelligibility of the target language, not a general accent lesson.

items: Write three phrases: next to a temple, opposite the bus stop, there’s a park.
Say each naturally. Ask learners to listen for joined words and small, weak words.
Mark stress and linking on the board (NEXT to a TEMple; there’s a PARK).
Class repeats chorally, then in pairs.
Move on. This is noticing, not a full pronunciation lesson (Unit 4).
Point to /ə/ on the class phonemic chart for the weak a and to.
Clap the stress pattern of each phrase.
Support: slow the phrase down first, then speed up.
Stretch: learners find another phrase from the description with the same pattern.

lines: NEXT tə ə TEMple → /ˈnekst tə ə ˈtempl/ (the to and a are weak)
OPPosite thə BUS stop
there’s ə PARK (there is contracted, a weak)

body: Purpose: to show stress and weak forms in the lesson’s phrases. Content: three phrases in large type with stressed syllables in bold capitals and large dots above them, weak syllables in smaller grey type, and linking arcs beneath. Style: clean typography. Board version: as described with chalk dots and arcs.

items: YouGlish (free). Play one or two clips of next to the to show the weak forms in real speech; choose clips in advance.

pts: Pre-teach only the lexical chunks that would otherwise block the task — resist the urge to front-load a long list.
Present each chunk in a short example sentence, not as an isolated translation pair.
Everything else is left for incidental pickup and later recycling, as Unit 5 recommends.

items: Pre-teach only the chunks needed for the task: next to, opposite, between … and …, behind, on the corner.
Present each chunk with the map: point and say, learners repeat.
Check meaning with one CCQ each (Opposite: are they on the same side of the road? No.).
Learners write the chunks in their notebooks with a small drawing.
Leave the chunks on the board in the vocabulary zone (Unit 9) for the rest of the lesson.
Use learners’ bodies: ‘Stand next to Asha. Stand opposite the door.’
Use objects on the desk (a pen between two books).
Support: pictures with the chunks.
Stretch: add at the end of, in front of, across from.

blocks.x: Chunks with examples from the description:

lines: next to a small temple / opposite the bus stop / between the pharmacy and the post office / behind the post office / on the corner

blocks.x: A home-language comparison: in Kannada, the equivalent of these words usually follows the noun (a postposition), as in bus stop-na eduru (‘opposite the bus stop’) [VERIFY transliteration with a Kannada speaker]. In English the word comes first. Pointing this out once helps learners notice the English order.

body: Purpose: a visual reference. Content: five small scenes, each with two simple buildings and a person: side by side (next to), across a road (opposite), a building between two others (between), one building behind another (behind), a building at a road junction (on the corner). Each labelled with the chunk. Style: consistent flat icons. Board version: boxes and a stick figure.

items: Wordwall (free basic version). A ‘Labelled diagram’ activity where learners drag chunks to the right position on a map.

blocks.x: Chunk cards held up by volunteers standing in position.

pts: Set a short consciousness-raising task: learners find and underline the target structure in the listening transcript.
Ask CCQs to confirm the meaning has landed before any explicit rule is offered.
Only supply the rule explicitly if the noticing task reveals a genuine gap, not as a default step.

v: The written description on the board or a handout

items: Show the written description. Learners underline every sentence beginning with There’s or There are.
Ask guiding questions: ‘What comes after There’s: one thing or many? What about There are?’
Pairs write the rule in one sentence.
Check with CCQs: There’s a park. How many parks? (One.)
Learners write two true sentences about their own neighbourhood using the pattern.
Add the question form: Is there a pharmacy near your house?
Add the negative: There isn’t a cinema.
Support: provide sentence halves to match.
Stretch: include some and any (There are some shops. There aren’t any cinemas.).

blocks.x: The pattern, drawn out by learners:

lines: One thing: There’s a pharmacy. (There is)
More than one: There are two schools.
Question: Is there a bus stop near your house? Yes, there is. / No, there isn’t.
T: Look at There’s a park and There are shops. What’s different?
S1: There’s for one. There are for many.
T: Good. Write that in your own words.

body: Purpose: to show the singular–plural contrast. Content: two panels. Left panel: a single park icon with the caption ‘There’s a park.’ Right panel: three shop icons with the caption ‘There are three shops.’ A small question panel beneath: ‘Is there a…? Are there any…?’ Style: bright, simple icons. Board version: one circle and three circles with captions.

items: Google Docs (free). Share the description; learners highlight the pattern and comment with their rule.

blocks.x: Printed or board text; learners underline in notebooks.

pts: Move into pair work quickly; give instructions in short, demonstrated steps with a quick ICQ check.
Monitor silently, noting patterns for later — this is where the delayed feedback of Unit 8 begins.
Teacher talk in this stage should be near zero outside of monitoring and brief redirection.

v: Blank paper; the chunks and pattern on the board

items: Instructions in three sentences (Unit 7): ‘Draw a map of your street. Don’t show your partner. Describe it; your partner draws it.’
Demonstrate with one learner: describe two places while they draw on the board.
ICQs: ‘Do you show your map? (No.) Who draws? (Your partner.)’ A quick Kannada check for anyone unsure.
Pairs work. Speaker A describes; B draws. Then swap.
Pairs compare maps and find differences.
Monitor silently, noting good language and errors on the three-column sheet (Unit 7).
In fixed benches, work with the partner beside you; a second round with the partner behind.
Describe the school instead of a street.
Support: the drawer may ask Is there a…? questions to help.
Stretch: include one ‘mistake’ in the description for the partner to catch.

lines: A: There’s a temple on the corner. Next to the temple, there’s a shop.
B: What kind of shop?
A: A vegetable shop. Opposite the shop, there are two houses.
B: Like this?
A: Yes!

blocks.x: Teacher talk during this stage should be almost nothing beyond the instructions and occasional prompts (Can you say where the park is?).

body: Purpose: to show the pair set-up. Content: two learners seated side by side, one holding a hidden map and speaking, the other drawing on paper. Speech bubble: ‘Opposite the shop, there are two houses.’ A teacher in the background with a clipboard, not speaking. Style: friendly classroom illustration. Board version: not applicable.

items: Classroomscreen (free basic version). A visible timer for each round.

blocks.x: A clap or hand signal to switch roles.

body: The draw-and-describe task has a genuine information gap (Unit 3), so learners must communicate to succeed. If you notice pairs simply showing each other their maps, remind them of the goal: the partner’s drawing should match without looking.

pts: End the lesson with feedback drawn from monitoring notes, focused on one recurring error type, not a full error list.
Praise specific, well-used language spotted during monitoring, not generic effort.
Add any recurring error to the learner's ongoing error log for tracking across future lessons.

items: From your monitoring notes, choose one recurring error related to the aim (for example, There is two shops).
Write two good sentences and two sentences with the error on the board.
Learners fix the errors in pairs; check using the correction hierarchy (Unit 8).
Give specific praise for good language you heard.
Learners add one correction to their error log.
Exit ticket: learners write two sentences describing where two places are in their neighbourhood and circle a face (☺ ● ☹).
Replace the exit ticket with a show-of-fingers check in very large classes.
Collect one learner-produced map to display, with permission.
Support: exit-ticket frame (There’s a ___ next to the ___.).
Stretch: exit ticket includes one question (Is there a…?).

lines: Good language: Between the school and the park, there’s a small shop. / Opposite my house, there are two trees.
Fix it: There is two shops. → There are two shops. / The temple is next the shop. → next to the shop.

blocks.x: Specific praise: Rahul used between … and … correctly and clearly. That’s a hard one.

body: Purpose: to show a feedback board with one focus. Content: a board divided into two columns (‘Good language’ with a tick; ‘Fix it’ with a wrench), four sentences, and a small highlighted box at the bottom labelled ‘Today’s focus: there is / there are’. Style: chalk-like, clean. Board version: as described.

items: Padlet (free plan). If learners have devices, collect exit tickets as short posts.

blocks.x: Paper exit-ticket slips collected at the door.

pts: Immediately after the lesson, note briefly what worked, what stalled, and why — while it's still fresh.
Feed that note directly into the next lesson's aim and staging, continuing the cycle Unit 9 described.
This is the mechanism by which Tier I's next fifteen posters will keep building on real classroom evidence.

v: Exit tickets; monitoring notes; lesson plan

items: Sort the exit tickets into three piles by face and by accuracy.
Answer the three reflection questions (Unit 9): what worked, what did not, what will change.
Add recurring errors to the class error pattern list.
Decide the aim of the next lesson, using the evidence. For example, if most learners succeeded, move on to giving directions; if many used there is with plurals, revisit briefly in the warmer.
Update learner profiles for any learner who stood out, positively or with difficulty.
Share the reflection with a colleague who teaches a parallel class.
Ask learners a one-question reflection: ‘What helped you most today?’
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: A reflection entry for this lesson:

lines: Worked: draw-and-describe; almost every pair finished and maps matched. 26 of 32 exit tickets correct.
Didn’t work: noticing-sounds stage felt rushed; some learners still say next the without to.
Change: warmer next lesson, 3 minutes of next to and opposite with objects on desks. Then: giving directions (Turn left, go straight on).

body: Purpose: a summary diagram of the whole checkpoint lesson. Content: a horizontal timeline of 60 minutes divided into coloured blocks for each stage (listening 10, sounds 5, chunks 7, grammar 10, pairs 18, feedback 10). Above each block, a small icon; above the whole line, a banner with the aim. Below the line, a curved arrow looping from the end back to the start labelled ‘reflect and re-plan’. Style: clean infographic, consistent colours with earlier figures. Board version: not applicable.

items: Google Forms (free). If exit tickets were digital, the summary view shows results instantly.

blocks.x: The sorted exit-ticket piles and a notebook page.

body: Teach this model lesson, or your own version of it, and ask a colleague to observe with one question in mind: at which stage did learners talk most? Compare the answer with your plan. The stage you expected to be most productive is not always the one that was.

dek: Unit 10 of 100: closing the Foundations opening arc by walking one lesson end-to-end, showing exactly where Units 1 through 9 meet inside a single 60-minute class.

aims.x: This checkpoint unit brings Units 1–9 together in one worked lesson. Each of the eight points below is one stage of the same sixty-minute lesson, so that you can see how the foundations fit together in practice rather than as separate topics.
By the end of this unit you should be able to:

items: plan a complete lesson that draws on learner profiles, listening, pronunciation, vocabulary, grammar, classroom craft, feedback and reflection;
explain how each stage prepares for the next;
adapt the model lesson to your own learners, level and timetable;
use reflection after the lesson to plan the next one.

why: Why this matters. Nine posters of separate foundations only prove their worth once they combine. This checkpoint is the proof of concept before Tier I goes deeper, poster by poster, to 25.

background.x: Checkpoints are where separate ideas are tested together. In the first nine units, each foundation was examined on its own: learners’ needs, the four skills, sounds, words, grammar, classroom craft, feedback and planning. In a real classroom, of course, they all happen at once. A teacher presenting a new structure is also managing talk time, reading the room, choosing which errors to correct and keeping one eye on the clock.

The model lesson in this unit is deliberately ordinary. Its topic is a neighbourhood, its level is A2, its learners are twelve to fourteen years old and it lasts sixty minutes, or a double period in many timetables. It could be taught with a blackboard and chalk alone. Nothing in it depends on special materials or technology, although each stage suggests a digital option where devices are available.

The lesson follows a familiar shape: a listening lead-in provides input, pronunciation and vocabulary work prepare learners to use it, a noticing task draws out the grammar, pair work gives practice, and feedback and reflection close the loop. Its aim, written as a can-do statement on the board from the first minute, is: Learners can describe where places are in their neighbourhood.
The list below summarizes the whole lesson. The eight points that follow take each stage in turn.

items: Before the lesson: use the learner profiles to decide level, examples and grouping (point 1).
Stage 1, 10 minutes: listening lead-in (point 2).
Stage 2, 5 minutes: noticing sounds (point 3).
Stage 3, 7 minutes: vocabulary in chunks (point 4).
Stage 4, 10 minutes: grammar through noticing (point 5).
Stage 5, 18 minutes: pair practice with minimal teacher talk (point 6).
Stage 6, 10 minutes: focused feedback and exit ticket (point 7).
After the lesson: reflect and re-plan (point 8).
Aim achievement. The exit tickets show directly how many learners reached the can-do. Record the figure.
Pair task outcome. Count the pairs whose drawn maps matched the described maps in most details.
Language use. From monitoring notes, count uses of the target chunks and the there is / there are pattern during pair work.
Follow-up retention. In the next lesson’s warmer, check whether the chunks are recalled without the board.
Which stage of the model lesson would be hardest in your context, and why?
How would you adapt the lesson for a class of sixty in fixed benches? For a class of adults?
Where in the lesson could learners’ home languages help most?
Which foundation from Units 1–9 do you think this lesson uses least well? How could it be strengthened?
What evidence would convince you that this lesson achieved its aim?

terms.def: A lesson aim written as what learners will be able to do by the end, such as ‘I can ask for and give directions to a place in my town.’
A lesson that brings together and reviews the language and skills taught in preceding lessons, allowing the teacher to check progress before moving on.
A short task learners complete at the end of a lesson, such as one sentence using the target language or an answer to a question. It gives the teacher quick evidence for planning the next lesson.
A way of teaching in which learners work out a rule or pattern from examples, guided by the teacher’s questions, rather than being told the rule first.
An activity in which learners hold different information and must communicate to complete a task, such as finding differences between two pictures or completing a timetable.

The short opening stage of a lesson that engages learners’ interest, activates what they already know about the topic and prepares them for the main input; for example, showing a photo of a local market before a shopping dialogue.
A word that follows a noun to show relations such as place or direction, as in Kannada and Hindi, where English uses a preposition before the noun; comparing these orders helps learners.
A preposition that shows where something is, such as in, on, under, next to or opposite; in English it comes before the noun, unlike the postpositions of Kannada or Hindi.
